Licenses

What Trycord is released under, what it is built from, and what the licence does not cover. The short version: the software is MIT licensed, and you can run, change and give it away.

1. The software

Trycord is released under the MIT licence. The full text is in the LICENSE file at the root of the repository, and it is the licence that applies to the server, the web client, the desktop client and the public website.

In short: you may use the software, including commercially; you may copy it, modify it, merge it into your own work, publish it, and distribute it; and you may sublicense it. The one condition is that the copyright notice and the permission notice travel with every copy or substantial portion of it.

The licence comes with no warranty. The software is provided as it is, and the responsibility for running it, and for what it does with other people's data, stays with whoever runs it.

2. The dependencies

The server is built on established libraries rather than on home-made versions of the parts that are hard to get right: password hashing, token signing, TLS-terminating proxies, database drivers, mail transport and the HTTP stack itself. Each dependency carries its own licence.

These are the direct dependencies of the server, with the licence each one carries. Every one of them is compatible with the MIT licence this project uses, and there is no copyleft anywhere in the tree.

The server's direct dependencies and their licences
PackageLicence
expressMIT
wsMIT
bcryptMIT
jsonwebtokenMIT

better-sqlite3MIT

dotenvBSD-2-Clause

The client carries one vendored library: @noble/curves (MIT), which supplies the elliptic-curve arithmetic its end-to-end encryption needs. It is vendored into the client rather than fetched from a content delivery network, because the client is served by the instance and must not depend on somebody else's host for the arithmetic its privacy rests on. Its licence text is in frontend/packages/vendor/LICENSE.noble-curves.

None of the core functionality requires a third-party account or a hosted service. Optional integrations, such as mail delivery, an object store for uploads, or a turn server for voice, are clearly marked and can be left unconfigured.

3. Fonts and artwork

The website and the clients use Manrope for text and JetBrains Mono for code. Both are distributed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, which permits use in a website or an application, including commercially. The licence text for both families is included with them in public/fonts/OFL.txt, and the copyright notices for both are in public/fonts/NOTICE.txt — the licence requires the notice of the copyright holder to travel with the font, and there are two families here.

The flame mark and the other artwork in this repository are part of the project and are covered by the MIT licence, with the exception of anything that came from somewhere else. The icon and the social preview image are in public/assets.

If you redistribute the site, keep the licence texts and the notices with it. That is what the fonts' licence asks for, and it is the polite thing to do with every dependency.

4. What the licence does not cover

The MIT licence covers the software. It does not cover the content people post on an instance, the names and logos of the communities on it, or the terms in the Terms of Service. Those are between the people who post them and the operator of the instance they are posted on.

It also does not make the project responsible for an instance. A self-hoster running this software is running their own service, under their own name, with their own obligations; the licence gives them permission to do that, and nothing more.

5. Your own instance

You may run an unmodified instance, a modified one, or one with your own code alongside it. If you modify the software and publish it, the published version is yours to license, provided the notices of the original work travel with it. If you keep the original name and mark, that implies the project endorses your version, which it does not; a fork with a different name is a different thing and does not need a permission to exist.

6. Trademarks

The MIT licence grants rights in the code. It does not grant rights in the name Trycord or in the flame mark, and it does not let anybody use them in a way that suggests a connection with the project that does not exist.

7. Contributions

A contribution you send to the project is accepted under the same MIT licence as the rest of the software. Say so when you send it, and do not send code you are not allowed to license this way. A change that is accepted is credited the way the project credits contributions generally, which is in the commit history.
